summary:
Isparta province stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Isparta-specific statute, incident, police action or court case appears in the sources behind this record, so the assessment below describes national law and national enforcement as they apply in Isparta alongside every other province.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend Turkey's penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality at up to three years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies at up to four years. The same package would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over, conditioned on infertility and repeated evaluations, and would expose medical providers to fines and up to seven years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to it.

Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records the enforcement a visitor would meet in any province. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans on the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. A court overturned the Istanbul governorate ban in November 2025 as disproportionate and unlawful, yet prosecutions of 92 people for taking part in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had acted outside its stated purpose and shared obscene images incompatible with the law.

Three draft law packages aimed at LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and would make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was submitted to parliament, and the leaked October package likewise remained unpassed, but the declared intent has not waited on enactment to shape how authorities act.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans visitor stopped, questioned or refused service has no statutory protection to invoke. Identity documents are compared against presentation at every checkpoint interaction, and the absence of any equality guarantee removes the legal ground on which a complaint would stand.
tangentialFactors:
Formal tolerance on paper has deep roots and now reads mainly as contrast: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, while the current trajectory runs in the opposite direction.

Pride events have been banned by governors in most years, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions deployed against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were prohibited by the cities' governors.

A February 2026 newspaper report stated that the government was considering a further law criminalising the public encouragement of behaviour contrary to biological sex, with a sentence of one to three years.

Adjacent measures show how far official policy extends beyond street enforcement: openly LGBT people are barred from military service under an armed forces health regulation defining homosexuality as a psychosexual illness, with conscripts who declare it required to provide photographic proof, and same-sex marriage is not recognised after a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Turkey since 1988, but residents live without a comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, in employment, housing, healthcare or public service.

The three draft law packages circulated in 2025 were never submitted to parliament, so the criminal penalties they propose, including the penalties for medical providers in the October package, are not in force; residents nonetheless face the healthcare restriction to age 25 with infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions as the stated direction of policy.

Civil society organising carries direct risk. The December 2025 Izmir court dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association shows that registration does not shield an LGBTI+ organisation from being wound up over its stated purpose and its published material.

Residents who take part in pride marches remain exposed to prosecution, with the 92 Istanbul cases still active at the end of 2025 despite the November ruling that the underlying ban was unlawful.

Military service is closed to openly LGBT people, and the declaration process itself requires photographic evidence of homosexuality.
outOfScopeNotes:
No local material for Isparta is sourced: police practice in the province, any Isparta pride or LGBTI+ organisation, local health facilities handling transition-related care, and local court decisions are all unaddressed by the documents behind this record.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package or any of the three packages circulated during 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; they are recorded as drafts and, for the three packages, as not submitted to parliament.

The February 2026 account of a further criminalising law rests on a single newspaper report and has not been corroborated against enacted text or an official draft.

The reach of the November 2025 court ruling annulling the Istanbul governorate ban beyond Istanbul, and the outcome of the 92 pending prosecutions, are not established by the sources available here.
